Monopoly spaces you can't buy.Mayfair: Mayfair is the most expensive space on the UK board, and a property you can buy.
Monopoly spaces you can't buy.Park Lane: Park Lane is the UK counterpart to Park Place, and it's purchasable.
Monopoly spaces you can't buy.Old Kent Road: The cheapest property on the UK board, and it can be bought for 60 pounds.
Monopoly spaces you can't buy.Pall Mall: Pall Mall is a pink property in the UK version, and it can be bought. It's pronounced 'pell mell'.
Monopoly spaces you can't buy.Bond Street: A green property in the UK version, and it can be bought.

Things with a screen.Smartphone: IBM's Simon, from 1994, had a touchscreen and is often called the first smartphone.
Things with a screen.Laptop: Laptops have screens that fold shut, protecting the display when you carry one.
Things with a screen.Television: Philo Farnsworth demonstrated the first all-electronic television in 1927 when he was just 21.
Things with a screen.Tablet: Tablets are nearly all screen, which is why they have so little else to look at.
Things with a screen.Smartwatch: Smartwatches show the time on a tiny screen, and some track your heart rate too.
Things with a screen.ATM: The first ATM was installed at Barclays in Enfield, north London, in 1967.
Things with a screen.Computer monitor: A monitor is basically all screen, and most use LED backlighting.
Things with a screen.E-reader: E Ink uses tiny charged capsules and draws power only when the page changes, which is why e-readers last weeks.
Things with a screen.Digital camera: Steven Sasson built the first digital camera at Kodak in 1975; it took 23 seconds to record one black-and-white image.
Things with a screen.Nintendo Switch: The Switch has sold well over 100 million units, a hybrid you can play docked or in your hands.
Things with a screen.Self-checkout: Self-checkouts have touch screens that talk you through scanning, and sometimes scold you.
Things with a screen.Sat nav: Satellite navigation relies on GPS satellites orbiting about 20,000 kilometers up.
Things with a screen.Typewriter: A typewriter has no screen; the paper itself is the display, and mistakes are permanent.
Things with a screen.Toaster: Even 'smart' toasters are rare, since most have just a dial.
Things with a screen.Rotary phone: A rotary phone has a dial, not a screen, and dialing a zero took the longest.
Things with a screen.Record player: A record player has a needle and a groove, not a screen.
Things with a screen.Abacus: An abacus is a calculating frame, and it has been used for thousands of years.
Things with a screen.Analog watch: An analog watch has a dial and hands, not a screen.
Things with a screen.Book: A book is the opposite of an e-reader, since its pages are printed paper.
Things with a screen.Mirror: A mirror reflects, though 'smart mirrors' with built-in displays exist.
Things with a screen.Kettle: A kettle has no screen, though some now have a temperature display.
Things with a screen.Sundial: A sundial uses shadows, so it needs sun and no screen.
Things with a screen.Compass: A compass has a magnetic needle, not a screen.
Things with a screen.Flashlight: A flashlight has a bulb or LED, and no screen, so it lights things rather than shows them.

Things you'd need to paint a room.Paint roller: The paint roller was invented in Toronto in 1940 by Norman Breakey, and it let one person cover a wall far faster than a brush.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Paintbrush: Natural-bristle brushes suit oil-based paint, while synthetic filament brushes are the better pick for water-based latex.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Drop cloth: Canvas drop cloths stay put and soak up drips, while plastic sheeting is slippery underfoot and leaves puddles.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Painter's tape: Masking tape was invented in 1925 by Richard Drew of 3M for car painters, and the Scotch name came from their gripes about stingy glue.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Paint tray: The ribbed ramp in the tray lets you roll off excess paint evenly so the roller does not drip on the way to the wall.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Stepladder: Most ladder falls come from overreaching, and the top step is not meant to be stood on.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Primer: Primer seals porous walls and gives topcoats something to grip, and a tinted primer helps cover a dark old color in fewer coats.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Sandpaper: Sandpaper is not made with sand anymore; the grit is usually aluminum oxide or silicon carbide, and a higher number means finer.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Stirring stick: Pigment and solids sink in a can, so stirring thoroughly keeps the color consistent from first wall to last.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Putty knife: A flexible blade lets it push filler flat into holes, and a stiff one scrapes off peeling paint.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Spackle: Spackle began as a brand name from the Muralo company, and many people now use it for any wall patching paste.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Paint can: The groove around the lid collects paint, so wiping it before closing keeps the seal clean and the can easy to open next time.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Plunger: A plunger works by moving water, not air, so the cup must be fully submerged to force a clog loose.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Whisk: Whisking beats air in, and trapped bubbles in paint leave tiny pockmarks, so painters stir gently with a stick.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Garden hose: Garden hoses use a standard thread size different from plumbing pipes, and they belong outdoors, not near fresh interior paint.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Ladle: The word comes from Old English for 'to load', and ladles were scooping soup long before anyone thought of paint.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Rolling pin: It looks like a roller, but a bare wooden cylinder has no fuzzy nap to hold paint, so it would smear a thin streaky mess.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Lint roller: The sticky lint roller was invented in 1956 by Nicholas McKay, who wanted a quick way to clean clothes.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Toilet brush: Its stiff, stubby bristles are built for scrubbing porcelain, and would leave deep streaks in wet paint.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Mop: A mop is handy for cleaning up afterwards, but it applies nothing to the walls and only spreads drips around on the floor.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Colander: The word comes from Latin colare, 'to strain', which is all a colander does; wet paint would simply flow through the holes.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Tongs: Tongs are among the oldest tools, first used by blacksmiths and cooks to handle things too hot to touch.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Hair straightener: Flat irons use heated plates, often ceramic, at around 180 degrees Celsius, far too hot for a painted wall.
Things you'd need to paint a room.Corkscrew: Corkscrews are thought to descend from the worm, a screw used to pull stuck bullets from musket barrels.

Things that hang from a ceiling.Chandelier: Chandeliers began as candle holders in medieval halls, and big crystal ones can weigh well over a ton, needing serious ceiling support.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Ceiling fan: A ceiling fan doesn't cool the air at all; it cools you, by moving air over skin so sweat evaporates faster.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Pendant light: Pendant lights dangle on a cord or rod, and designers usually hang one about 30 inches above a table so it lights without blocking views.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Baby mobile: Baby mobiles are often black and white or red because newborns can't see fine detail, but they respond to strong contrast.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Disco ball: The disco ball dates to 1917 but got famous in the 1970s; it is a sphere covered in hundreds of small mirrors, which scatter light spots.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Hanging plant: Spider plants are a favorite for hanging baskets, and they send out long stems that dangle baby plantlets.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Bat: Bats roost upside down because their legs are too thin for a running take-off, so they just drop into flight; their feet lock with tendons.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Stalactite: Stalactites hang from cave ceilings and grow roughly an inch per century; to remember, 'c' for ceiling and 'ite' for tight to it.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Punching bag: Heavy bags hang from a chain or strap, and boxers train on them to build power, and speed bags to build rhythm and timing.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Paper lantern: Paper lanterns have been used in China for over 2,000 years, and lantern festivals mark the end of Lunar New Year celebrations.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Rug: Rugs lie on the floor, and the oldest surviving one, the Pazyryk carpet, is about 2,400 years old and was preserved in Siberian ice.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Doormat: A doormat belongs on the ground; the standard 'Welcome' mat is a modern invention, and its coir fibers come from coconut husks.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Sofa: A sofa sits on the floor, and its name comes from the Arabic 'suffa', a bench, which reached Europe via the Ottoman world.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Coffee table: A coffee table sits low to the floor, and it only took off in the early 1900s as people began serving tea and coffee in the living room.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Bathtub: A bathtub is a floor fixture; a full one with a person can weigh over 500 pounds, so no ceiling could hold it.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Floor lamp: A floor lamp stands on the ground by definition, and many torchiere designs bounce light up off the ceiling.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Bookcase: A bookcase stands on the floor, and tall ones are usually bolted to the wall because they can tip over when loaded.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Fridge: A fridge belongs on the floor, and the average one weighs well over 200 pounds when empty.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Double bed: A double bed sits on the floor, though bunk and loft beds do raise it up, and some canopy beds hang drapes from the ceiling.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Toilet: A toilet is bolted to the floor; the Victorian plumber Thomas Crapper popularized flush toilets, though he did not invent them.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Washing machine: A washing machine stands on the floor; a front-loader spins at about 1,000 revolutions a minute, so it must be firmly grounded.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Treadmill: A treadmill rests on the floor, and it began as a Victorian prison punishment where inmates walked a wheel.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Stalagmite: This is the trap: a stalagmite grows up from the cave floor, while the stalactite hangs from the ceiling; 'mites' rise, 'tites' hold tight.
Things that hang from a ceiling.Floor tile: A floor tile is by name for the floor, but some historic buildings do have ceiling tiles of the same fired clay.

Things that have a neck.Bottle: A bottle's neck is the narrow part that makes pouring easier, and the shape helps to control the flow and to hold a cork.
Things that have a neck.Guitar: A guitar's neck holds the frets, and a pre-modern neck was often made of mahogany, with a metal truss rod added inside.
Things that have a neck.Violin: The violin's neck has no frets, so players must find each note by ear, and a tiny shift changes the pitch.
Things that have a neck.Giraffe: A giraffe has only seven neck vertebrae, the same number as humans, but each can be over 10 inches long.
Things that have a neck.Swan: A swan's long neck lets it reach plants deep underwater, and it has 22 to 25 vertebrae, far more than most birds.
Things that have a neck.Ukulele: The ukulele's name means 'jumping flea' in Hawaiian, and its short neck gives it a bright, small sound.
Things that have a neck.Cello: A cello's neck ends in a scroll, and the player holds it between the knees, with an endpin resting on the floor.
Things that have a neck.Banjo: The banjo's neck is long, and its roots go back to West African instruments brought over by enslaved people.
Things that have a neck.Flamingo: Flamingos have a long, S-shaped neck, and they can rest by standing on one leg to save body heat.
Things that have a neck.Ostrich: An ostrich's neck helps make it the tallest bird, up to about nine feet, but contrary to myth it doesn't bury its head in sand.
Things that have a neck.Turtleneck: A turtleneck has a high, folded collar around the neck, and its name is a nod to a turtle pulling its head in.
Things that have a neck.Plate: A plate has a rim and a base, but no neck, and the word dates to the Old French for 'flat piece'.
Things that have a neck.Drum: A drum has a shell and a head, but no neck, which is where the term 'drumhead' comes from.
Things that have a neck.Bowl: A bowl has a rim and a base, and no neck, but a bottle-shaped vase does.
Things that have a neck.Mug: A mug has a handle and a rim, and no neck, and the word likely came from a Scandinavian term for a pot.
Things that have a neck.Piano: A piano has strings, keys, and a soundboard, and no neck, and it's classed as a keyboard instrument that's also percussion.
Things that have a neck.Tambourine: A tambourine has a frame and jingles but no neck, and it appears in ancient art from Egypt and Mesopotamia.
Things that have a neck.Frisbee: A Frisbee has a rim and a flat top, no neck, and it was inspired by pie tins from the Frisbie Baking Company.
Things that have a neck.Pancake: A pancake is flat and round with no neck, and the world's tallest stack was well over 100 pancakes high.
Things that have a neck.Brick: A brick is a block with no neck, and the oldest known bricks are mud ones from around 9000 BCE.
Things that have a neck.Jellyfish: A jellyfish has a bell and tentacles but no neck, and a few kinds are thought to be biologically immortal.
Things that have a neck.Starfish: A starfish has arms, but no neck, and it can regrow a lost arm; sometimes a lost arm can even grow into a whole new starfish.
Things that have a neck.Worm: A worm has no neck, though it has a clitellum, a thick band, which is not a neck, and which holds reproductive organs.
Things that have a neck.Shoebox: A shoebox has a lid and a base but no neck, and shoeboxes are a classic place to store old photographs.

Things that smell bad.Garbage: The smell of garbage comes from bacteria breaking down food and releasing sulfur compounds, which our noses detect in tiny amounts.
Things that smell bad.Sweaty socks: Sweat itself is almost odorless; the smell appears when skin bacteria break it down, and feet have about 250,000 sweat glands.
Things that smell bad.Rotten eggs: The rotten-egg smell is hydrogen sulfide, which we can sniff at tiny levels, and gas companies add similar scents to natural gas.
Things that smell bad.Skunk: A skunk sprays a sulfur-rich oil called thiol from glands near its tail, and it can hit a target from about 10 feet away.
Things that smell bad.Sour milk: Milk turns sour as bacteria make lactic acid from its sugar, and that acid also makes buttermilk and yogurt.
Things that smell bad.Litter box: Cat urine gets its sharp smell partly from a compound called felinine, and it gets stronger as ammonia builds up.
Things that smell bad.Wet dog: Wet dog smell comes from bacteria and yeast on the fur, and water makes their smelly gases evaporate into the air.
Things that smell bad.Dirty diaper: Diapers smell because gut bacteria produce compounds like skatole, which in tiny amounts is used in perfumes.
Things that smell bad.Compost bin: A healthy compost pile smells earthy, and a stinky one is usually missing air or holding too many wet scraps.
Things that smell bad.Clogged drain: Drain smells come from rotting buildup that gives off hydrogen sulfide and other gases, which is why they smell like sewage.
Things that smell bad.Gym bag: Gym bags smell because damp clothes grow bacteria, and a cheap trick is to leave the bag open to air out between visits.
Things that smell bad.Fresh bread: The smell of baking bread is so appealing that some bakeries and shops pump it out to attract buyers.
Things that smell bad.Roses: Rose scent comes from compounds like geraniol, and it takes about 10,000 petals to produce a single gram of rose oil.
Things that smell bad.Lavender: Lavender's scent comes from linalool, and studies suggest the aroma can slightly reduce anxiety and help with sleep.
Things that smell bad.Clean laundry: The smell of clean laundry mostly comes from added fragrance, and truly clean fabric has little smell of its own.
Things that smell bad.Vanilla: Vanilla comes from a type of orchid, and it's the second most expensive spice after saffron, because pods are pollinated by hand.
Things that smell bad.Coffee beans: Coffee smells of over 800 aroma compounds, more than wine, which is part of why the smell alone can be energizing.
Things that smell bad.Cinnamon: Cinnamon's smell comes largely from cinnamaldehyde, and it's often used in air fresheners to make homes smell warm.
Things that smell bad.Baby powder: Baby powder's familiar scent is mostly added fragrance, and it pairs with talc or cornstarch, which absorb moisture.
Things that smell bad.Lemon: Lemon's zesty smell comes from limonene in the peel, and it's so strong that it is used in many cleaning products.
Things that smell bad.Cut grass: The smell of fresh-cut grass is a chemical alarm: the plant releases green leaf volatiles when it is injured.
Things that smell bad.Scented candle: Scented candles use fragrance oils mixed with wax, and some burn hotter than a plain one, which affects how far the scent travels.
Things that smell bad.Pine needles: Pine's smell comes from terpenes like pinene, which the trees release, and which contribute to the scent of forest air.
Things that smell bad.Fabric softener: Fabric softener coats fibers with a slippery layer and adds a long-lasting fragrance, which is why laundry stays scented.

Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Matches: Matches were invented in the 1820s by English chemist John Walker, who never patented them, and kids find fire irresistible.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Bleach: Bleach and ammonia cleaners produce toxic fumes if combined, so keep them locked up, and never in a drink bottle.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Kitchen knives: A toddler can reach a counter edge in no time, so knives should be stored high or in locked drawers.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Medicine: Child-resistant caps help but are not childproof, and most poisonings come from medicines left on a nightstand or in a purse.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Lighter: Lighters are a leading cause of child-played fires, and laws require child-resistant ones in many countries.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Button batteries: A swallowed coin cell can burn the throat in two hours, because saliva triggers a current, making it a real emergency.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Plastic bags: Thin film bags cause suffocation, and that is why many carry a warning label about keeping them away from babies.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Rat poison: Rodenticides are designed to attract, so these baits are risky, and they should be stored in sealed, high places.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Power tools: Even unplugged, tools have cutting edges, and cordless ones can start with a bump of the trigger.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Detergent pods: The bright squishy look of laundry pods, like candy, led to thousands of poisonings and prompted safer, opaque packaging.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Razor: Blades are sharp enough to cut skin with a light touch, which is why razors belong on a high shelf.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Superglue: Cyanoacrylate was discovered by accident in 1942 during wartime research on gunsights, and it can bond skin in seconds.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Teddy bear: The teddy is named for Theodore Roosevelt, after a 1902 hunting trip where he refused to shoot a tied-up bear.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Crayons: Crayons are made of nontoxic wax, and the first box from 1903 had eight colors costing a nickel.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Picture book: Reading aloud even to babies helps language development, and a sturdy board book can handle drool and tearing.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Building blocks: Friedrich Froebel, who invented the kindergarten, made blocks a learning tool in the 1830s, and they remain a classic.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Sippy cup: A spill-proof cup is meant for toddlers, so this one belongs in their hands.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Bib: A bib is kid gear, and a modern silicone one has a pocket to catch the food a toddler drops.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Rattle: Rattles are made to be safe, though a rattle with loose beads inside can be a choking risk if it breaks.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Pacifier: Pacifiers made for babies are designed with a shield too big to swallow, for safety.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Blanket: A loved blanket is known as a transitional object, and it can comfort a child through changes.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Rubber duck: Rubber ducks became a bath fixture in the 1940s, and in 1992 a spill of toys at sea was used to study ocean currents.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Jigsaw puzzle: The first jigsaw was a map cut by John Spilsbury in the 1760s as a geography teaching aid, and large piece sets suit toddlers.
Things to keep out of a toddler's reach.Play-Doh: Play-Doh began in the 1930s as a wallpaper cleaner, and it is basically flour, salt and water, so it is nontoxic if tasted.

Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Magic wand: A magic wand is a wizard's tool, and wands long predate fiction: ancient Egyptians carried wand-like staffs for protection.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Spellbook: A spellbook, or grimoire, is a wizard's reference, and real medieval grimoires listed spells to summon spirits and cure ills.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Pointy hat: The pointy hat is the wizard's silhouette, and tall conical hats are part of a long storybook tradition of mystical headwear.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Crystal ball: A crystal ball is for scrying, and the practice of gazing in a polished sphere goes back to ancient times for fortune-tellers.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Robe: A wizard's robe is long and flowing, and star-and-moon patterns are a popular fairy-tale touch on it.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Staff: A staff is a wizard's walking stick and focus, and Gandalf's from 'The Lord of the Rings' is among the best known.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Potion: A potion is a brewed liquid with magical effect, and ancient 'philters' were love potions that sometimes poisoned their drinkers.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Magic scroll: A magic scroll holds a spell in writing, and in ancient times scrolls of papyrus were the main form of book.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Cloak: A cloak is for traveling and hiding, and an invisibility cloak is a staple trick for storybook heroes and wizards.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Smartphone: A smartphone breaks the fairy-tale spell, since a wizard in a world of swords and candles wouldn't have anything electronic.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Jet ski: A jet ski needs an engine and fuel, and the first one was built by Clayton Jacobson in the 1960s, long after any fairy tale's era.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Hair straightener: A hair straightener runs on electricity, and fairy-tale wizards are known for a flowing beard rather than styled hair.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Microwave: A microwave oven was invented by accident in 1945 when Percy Spencer noticed a candy bar melting in his pocket near radar equipment.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Treadmill: A treadmill was first a punishment device in 19th-century prisons, not a fairy-tale item for a wizard's tower.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Selfie stick: A selfie stick is entirely modern, and a wizard would sooner use a scrying crystal for a portrait than one of these.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Electric guitar: An electric guitar doesn't fit a medieval wizard, and the first commercial ones appeared in the 1930s.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Game console: A game console is a modern gadget, and the first home console, the Magnavox Odyssey, appeared in 1972.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Drone: A drone is a flying robot, and a fairy-tale wizard would more likely send an owl to deliver a message.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Electric scooter: An electric scooter needs a battery, and a wizard would ride a broom or a dragon instead in most stories.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Sports car: A sports car needs an engine, and in the age of fairy tales the fastest ride was a horse.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Bluetooth speaker: A Bluetooth speaker is named after Harald Bluetooth, a Viking king, but wizards hear their music live.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Smartwatch: A smartwatch is a modern wearable, and a wizard keeping time in a fairy tale would use the sun or an hourglass.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Laptop: A laptop is a modern machine, and a fairy-tale wizard keeps knowledge in books and scrolls instead.
Things a fairy-tale wizard owns.Leaf blower: A leaf blower is a gas or electric tool from the 1950s, and a wizard would just wave his wand to clear the leaves.

Plumber's tools.Plunger: A plunger relies on air pressure: pushing forces water down, and the pull creates a vacuum.
Plumber's tools.Pipe wrench: A pipe wrench's jaws bite harder as you pull on the handle, making it perfect for round pipes.
Plumber's tools.Plumber's tape: Plumber's tape, or PTFE tape, is made of Teflon, and it seals threaded joints against leaks.
Plumber's tools.Drain snake: A drain snake is a flexible auger that works its way down the pipe to break up clogs.
Plumber's tools.Pipe cutter: A pipe cutter scores pipe as it rotates, giving a cleaner cut than a saw.
Plumber's tools.Basin wrench: A basin wrench has a swiveling head, so you can reach nuts in tight spots behind a sink.
Plumber's tools.Plumber's putty: Plumber's putty is a soft, oily clay that seals around drains and faucets, and it never fully hardens.
Plumber's tools.Tube bender: A tube bender curves copper pipe without kinking it, so plumbers avoid extra joints.
Plumber's tools.Pliers: Pliers grip pipes and fittings, and slip-joint types adjust to different sizes.
Plumber's tools.Stethoscope: A stethoscope listens to heartbeats and lungs; Laennec invented it in 1816, and plumbers use something similar only to hear leaks in walls.
Plumber's tools.Whisk: A whisk blends batter in the kitchen, and a plumber's bag holds nothing so delicate.
Plumber's tools.Easel: An easel props up a canvas for painting, and it's a studio item rather than a toolbox one.
Plumber's tools.Gavel: A gavel is a judge's or auctioneer's mallet, so it belongs to a courtroom, not a pipe job.
Plumber's tools.Scalpel: A scalpel is a surgeon's precision blade, sharper than most household knives, and wrong for cutting pipes.
Plumber's tools.Rolling pin: A rolling pin flattens dough for pies and pasta, and has no use in plumbing.
Plumber's tools.Paintbrush: A paintbrush is for coats of paint, and a plumber's job ends before the walls are decorated.
Plumber's tools.Sickle: A sickle is a curved blade for reaping grain, a farm tool that goes back thousands of years.
Plumber's tools.Trowel: A trowel is for gardeners and masons, who use it to spread mortar; it won't fix a leaky pipe.
Plumber's tools.Chisel: A chisel carves wood or stone, and plumbers use one only occasionally to open up walls.
Plumber's tools.Telescope: A telescope brings distant objects closer; Galileo improved it in 1609, but a plumber's work is close at hand.
Plumber's tools.Ladle: A ladle scoops soup, and plumbers know it as nothing but a kitchen tool that sometimes falls down drains.
Plumber's tools.Microphone: A microphone captures sound, and no plumber's kit includes one, even though plumbing can be loud.
Plumber's tools.Scissors: Scissors cut paper and cloth, and a plumber's copper pipe needs a proper pipe cutter instead.
Plumber's tools.Abacus: An abacus is a bead-based counting frame, thousands of years old, and it has no place in a plumber's kit.

Programming languages.Python: Named after Monty Python's Flying Circus rather than the snake, Python was created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991.
Programming languages.Java: Originally called Oak, it was renamed after coffee; its slogan 'write once, run anywhere' described its bytecode idea.
Programming languages.Ruby: Created by Yukihiro Matsumoto in Japan in the 1990s, it was named after a gemstone, as a nod to Perl, the pearl.
Programming languages.Rust: Started as a side project by Graydon Hoare at Mozilla, it gives memory safety without a garbage collector.
Programming languages.Go: Created at Google in 2009 by Robert Griesemer, Rob Pike and Ken Thompson, who also helped create Unix and C.
Programming languages.Swift: Apple introduced it in 2014 as a replacement for Objective-C when building iPhone and Mac apps.
Programming languages.Kotlin: Named after an island near St. Petersburg, it was made by JetBrains and became Google's preferred language for Android in 2019.
Programming languages.JavaScript: Brendan Eich wrote the first version in about ten days in 1995, and despite the name it has little to do with Java.
Programming languages.Perl: Larry Wall made it for text processing, and its motto is 'There's more than one way to do it.'
Programming languages.Haskell: Named for the logician Haskell Curry, it is a purely functional language that has inspired many mainstream features.
Programming languages.Fortran: Created at IBM in the 1950s, its name means Formula Translation, and it is still used in weather and physics models.
Programming languages.COBOL: Developed in 1959 with help from Grace Hopper, it still runs enormous numbers of banking and government systems.
Programming languages.Lua: Created in Brazil in 1993, its name means moon in Portuguese, and it's used to script games like Roblox.
Programming languages.HTML: It marks up web pages but isn't programming: it describes structure and has no logic of its own.
Programming languages.Linux: A kernel started by Linus Torvalds in 1991, an operating system and not a programming language, which most of the internet runs on.
Programming languages.Windows: Microsoft's operating system, which the programming languages are used to write, not one itself.
Programming languages.Excel: A spreadsheet program, though its formulas and macros have become a form of programming for millions.
Programming languages.Photoshop: Image-editing software that began in the late 1980s as a hobby project by brothers Thomas and John Knoll.
Programming languages.Firefox: A browser that's written in languages like C++ and Rust, which makes it a program rather than a language.
Programming languages.Bluetooth: A wireless standard named after the Viking king Harald Bluetooth, who united parts of Denmark and Norway.
Programming languages.JPEG: A compression format for photos, named after the Joint Photographic Experts Group that designed it.
Programming languages.Chrome: Google's browser, built from many programming languages but not itself one.
Programming languages.Ethernet: A wired networking standard invented at Xerox PARC in the 1970s, and the name nods to the old idea of the ether.
Programming languages.Unix: A family of operating systems born at Bell Labs in 1969, and it's the system C was created to write.

Audio file extensions..mp3: MP3 compression, developed in Germany at the Fraunhofer Institute, shrinks music about tenfold by discarding sounds people barely hear. It sparked the digital music revolution.
Audio file extensions..wav: WAV is a Microsoft and IBM format from 1991 that stores uncompressed audio. It's large, and it's still widely used in recording studios.
Audio file extensions..flac: FLAC means Free Lossless Audio Codec. It compresses audio to roughly half its size with no loss, so audiophiles favor it.
Audio file extensions..aac: AAC was designed as MP3's successor and generally sounds better at the same size. It's the default for Apple music and YouTube audio.
Audio file extensions..ogg: Ogg is an open, patent-free container, often holding the Vorbis codec. The name has nothing to do with the monsters called ogres.
Audio file extensions..m4a: M4A is usually AAC audio inside an MPEG-4 container, and it's what iTunes bought songs used. The 4 refers to MPEG-4.
Audio file extensions..wma: Windows Media Audio is Microsoft's rival to MP3, released in 1999. It had copy-protection features that annoyed some users.
Audio file extensions..aiff: AIFF is Apple's uncompressed audio format from 1988, a counterpart to Microsoft's WAV. Pro audio software still reads it.
Audio file extensions..mid: A MIDI file holds no sound at all, only instructions telling instruments which notes to play. That's why MIDI files are so tiny.
Audio file extensions..jpg: JPG is an image format named for the Joint Photographic Experts Group. It's about pictures, not sound.
Audio file extensions..png: PNG was created in the 1990s as a patent-free alternative to GIF. It holds images, and the letters stand for Portable Network Graphics.
Audio file extensions..docx: .docx is Microsoft Word's document format, which has been a zipped bundle of XML files since 2007. It stores text, not audio.
Audio file extensions..pdf: PDF, Portable Document Format, was created by Adobe in 1993 to keep pages looking the same everywhere. It holds documents, not sound.
Audio file extensions..gif: GIF dates back to 1987 and is famous for short looping animations. Its creators said it's pronounced with a soft g, which people still argue about.
Audio file extensions..mov: MOV is Apple's QuickTime video container. It can hold audio too, but it's mainly a video file.
Audio file extensions..avi: AVI is a video format Microsoft introduced in 1992. It mostly carries video, so the sound is a sidekick.
Audio file extensions..exe: EXE marks an executable program on Windows. Opening one runs code, which is why unknown ones deserve caution.
Audio file extensions..zip: ZIP archives compress and bundle files together, and the format dates to 1989. It can hold songs, but it isn't an audio format itself.
Audio file extensions..txt: TXT files hold plain text with no formatting, and they can be opened by nearly any program. They're about as simple as files get.
Audio file extensions..html: HTML is the markup language for web pages, created by Tim Berners-Lee around 1990. It describes pages, not sound.
Audio file extensions..psd: PSD is Photoshop's native layered image format. It stores artwork, not audio.
Audio file extensions..csv: CSV stands for comma-separated values, a simple text format for spreadsheet data. It stores tables, not sound.
Audio file extensions..mkv: MKV is the Matroska container, which can hold many video, audio and subtitle tracks. It's mostly used for video, so it's not an audio format.
Audio file extensions..wmv: WMV is Windows Media Video, a Microsoft video format. It shares a family with WMA but is for video.

Characters in Othello.Othello: The Moorish general in Venice is undone by jealousy and is one of the few Black protagonists in Shakespeare.
Characters in Othello.Iago: The ensign and villain who manipulates everyone around him, and has more lines than Othello himself.
Characters in Othello.Desdemona: She is killed by her husband after a lost handkerchief becomes the supposed proof of her adultery.
Characters in Othello.Cassio: The lieutenant is falsely accused of an affair with Desdemona, and loses his post after Iago gets him drunk.
Characters in Othello.Emilia: Iago's wife exposes his plot after Desdemona's death, and Iago kills her for it.
Characters in Othello.Roderigo: A rich Venetian gull who pays Iago to help him win Desdemona, and is used for his money.
Characters in Othello.Bianca: The courtesan who loves Cassio and unwittingly gets caught up in the handkerchief plot.
Characters in Othello.Brabantio: Desdemona's father, a Venetian senator who warns Othello: she deceived you, and may deceive you too.
Characters in Othello.Lodovico: Desdemona's relative who arrives from Venice with news at the play's end.
Characters in Othello.Shylock: The moneylender of The Merchant of Venice, who demands a pound of flesh, not an Othello character.
Characters in Othello.Portia: The clever heroine of The Merchant of Venice, who argues the case in court disguised as a lawyer.
Characters in Othello.Bassanio: Portia's suitor in The Merchant of Venice, who borrows money from Antonio to win her.
Characters in Othello.King Lear: The title king of a different tragedy, who divides his kingdom among his daughters.
Characters in Othello.Edgar: The son of Gloucester in King Lear, who spends part of the play disguised as Poor Tom.
Characters in Othello.Kent: King Lear's loyal servant, banished for telling him the truth, and then returns in disguise.
Characters in Othello.Gloucester: The earl in King Lear whose eyes are put out on stage.
Characters in Othello.Brutus: The Roman conspirator in Julius Caesar who agonizes over killing his friend.
Characters in Othello.Mark Antony: He is the Roman general in Julius Caesar and Antony and Cleopatra, and not part of Othello.
Characters in Othello.Macduff: The Scottish thane in Macbeth, who kills the king for the crown, and then is killed by Macduff.
Characters in Othello.Banquo: The murdered friend whose ghost haunts Macbeth's feast, not part of Othello.
Characters in Othello.Tybalt: Juliet's hot-tempered cousin, not a character in Othello.
Characters in Othello.Falstaff: The comic knight of the Henry plays and The Merry Wives of Windsor, not in Othello.
Characters in Othello.Prince Hal: The future Henry V is a wayward prince in Henry IV.
Characters in Othello.Antonio: The merchant of The Merchant of Venice, whose loan sets the plot in motion.

Classic Russian novels.War and Peace: Tolstoy's 1869 epic follows several families through the Napoleonic wars; it runs well over 1,000 pages in most editions.
Classic Russian novels.Anna Karenina: Opens with the famous line about happy families all being alike; Tolstoy's 1870s novel ends with a train station tragedy.
Classic Russian novels.Crime and Punishment: Dostoevsky's 1866 novel follows Raskolnikov, a student who commits murder, and his guilt-ridden unraveling.
Classic Russian novels.The Idiot: Dostoevsky's tale of a kind, naive prince, who is nearly saintly, shows how society treats goodness.
Classic Russian novels.Dead Souls: Gogol's 1842 satire follows a swindler buying the names of dead serfs; its title plays on the word souls.
Classic Russian novels.Fathers and Sons: Turgenev's 1862 novel gave the world the word 'nihilist' in its modern sense through the hero Bazarov.
Classic Russian novels.Doctor Zhivago: Pasternak's 1957 novel was smuggled out of the USSR for publication; he won the Nobel Prize but was forced to decline it.
Classic Russian novels.Eugene Onegin: Pushkin's verse novel was written over about eight years; Tchaikovsky turned it into an opera.
Classic Russian novels.Oblomov: Goncharov's 1859 novel stars a man so lazy that he barely leaves his bed or sofa for the first section.
Classic Russian novels.Resurrection: Tolstoy's last major novel, from 1899, follows a nobleman seeking redemption after wronging a servant girl.
Classic Russian novels.Les Misérables: Victor Hugo's 1862 French novel about Jean Valjean is not Russian, but it is just as sweeping as Tolstoy.
Classic Russian novels.Madame Bovary: Flaubert's 1857 French novel about Emma Bovary led to him being put on trial for obscenity.
Classic Russian novels.Don Quixote: Spanish, by Cervantes, 1605 and 1615, often called the first modern novel; it is not Russian.
Classic Russian novels.The Trial: Kafka wrote this unfinished German novel about a man arrested for no stated reason; it was published after his death.
Classic Russian novels.Ulysses: Joyce's 1922 Irish novel follows one day in Dublin, June 16, now celebrated as Bloomsday.
Classic Russian novels.Moby-Dick: Melville's 1851 novel, American, begins with 'Call me Ishmael', and is nothing like Russian novels.
Classic Russian novels.Candide: Voltaire's 1759 French satire follows an optimist through disasters, ending with the advice to cultivate our garden.
Classic Russian novels.The Stranger: Camus's 1942 French novel opens with 'Maman died today' and was written in Algeria's French culture.
Classic Russian novels.Faust: Goethe's German play about a scholar who bargains with the devil took him most of his life to finish.
Classic Russian novels.Germinal: Zola's 1885 French novel on striking coal miners is a landmark of naturalism.
Classic Russian novels.The Three Musketeers: Dumas's 1844 French adventure, where d'Artagnan joins the musketeers, was first serialized in a newspaper.
Classic Russian novels.Siddhartha: Hesse's 1922 German tale follows a young man's spiritual quest in ancient India.
Classic Russian novels.The Name of the Rose: Umberto Eco's 1980 Italian medieval murder mystery is set in a monastery, and is not Russian.
Classic Russian novels.Middlemarch: George Eliot's 1871 English novel was finished long after the Russian classics began; she wasn't Russian.

Mice in children's books.Reepicheep: The valiant talking mouse in C. S. Lewis's Narnia books carries a tiny sword and sails to the world's end in The Voyage of the Dawn Treader.
Mice in children's books.Despereaux: Kate DiCamillo's tiny, big-eared hero loves music and a princess; The Tale of Despereaux won the 2004 Newbery Medal.
Mice in children's books.Mrs. Frisby: The widowed field mouse in Robert C. O'Brien's novel seeks help from super-intelligent lab rats; the book won the 1972 Newbery Medal.
Mice in children's books.Angelina Ballerina: Katharine Holabird and Helen Craig's dancing mouse debuted in a 1983 picture book that grew into a long-running TV series.
Mice in children's books.Mrs. Tittlemouse: Beatrix Potter's fussy wood mouse is forever tidying her burrow, which keeps getting invaded by messy guests like Mr. Jackson the toad.
Mice in children's books.Maisy: Lucy Cousins' bold, black-outlined mouse has starred in toddler books since 1990 that have sold many millions of copies worldwide.
Mice in children's books.Geronimo Stilton: He is both the hero and the pen name of a series about a mouse editor in New Mouse City, translated into dozens of languages.
Mice in children's books.Ralph S. Mouse: Beverly Cleary's mouse rides a toy motorcycle, but it only goes if he makes the engine noise himself, 'pb-pb-b-b-b'.
Mice in children's books.Hunca Munca: In Beatrix Potter's The Tale of Two Bad Mice she and Tom Thumb wreck a dollhouse, discovering the dolls' food is just painted plaster.
Mice in children's books.Templeton: The greedy rat in Charlotte's Web is no mouse: he only helps Wilbur when he's promised first pick of the leftovers.
Mice in children's books.Scabbers: Ron Weasley's pet rat is not a mouse, and turns out to be Peter Pettigrew, the Animagus who betrayed Harry's parents.
Mice in children's books.Ratty: The gentle Water Rat in The Wind in the Willows is a rat, or really a water vole, which is why he loves messing about in boats.
Mice in children's books.Mole: The shy hero who opens The Wind in the Willows by abandoning spring cleaning is a mole, not a mouse, and a loyal friend to Ratty.
Mice in children's books.Peter Rabbit: Beatrix Potter's naughty rabbit loses his blue jacket in Mr. McGregor's garden; he is a rabbit, not a mouse.
Mice in children's books.Mrs. Tiggy-Winkle: Beatrix Potter based her laundry-washing hedgehog on a real Scottish washerwoman, and she is not a mouse.
Mice in children's books.Squirrel Nutkin: Potter's cheeky red squirrel riddles the owl Old Brown and loses his tail for it; the whole book is a squirrel's story.
Mice in children's books.Mr. Fox: Roald Dahl's Fantastic Mr Fox outwits three farmers who dig for him; he is a fox, so he doesn't belong with mice.
Mice in children's books.Piglet: Pooh's smallest friend is a very small animal who is a pig, famous for his nervousness, so he is no mouse.
Mice in children's books.Roo: Kanga's joey in the Hundred Acre Wood is a kangaroo, and he is the youngest of A. A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh gang.
Mice in children's books.Wilbur: The rescued pig in Charlotte's Web is saved by a spider's words, and he is a pig, not a mouse.
Mice in children's books.Remy: The Parisian chef-rat of Pixar's Ratatouille is a rat, who steers a human cook by pulling his hair.
Mice in children's books.Fiver: The small, psychic rabbit in Richard Adams' Watership Down foresees the doom of the warren, and he is a rabbit.
Mice in children's books.Mr. Toad: The boastful motor-car-mad squire of Toad Hall in The Wind in the Willows is a toad, not a mouse.

Things that are usually green.Grass: Grass is green thanks to chlorophyll, and a lawn is a field of plants that grow from their base, so mowing doesn't kill them.
Things that are usually green.Lime: Limes are green because they are picked before they ripen; fully ripe limes turn yellow.
Things that are usually green.Emerald: Emerald is a green beryl colored by chromium, and the gem has been prized since ancient Egypt, in Cleopatra's mines.
Things that are usually green.Broccoli: Broccoli is an Italian-bred cultivar of wild cabbage, and the word comes from the Italian for 'flowering crest'.
Things that are usually green.Cucumber: Cucumbers are about 95% water, and the plant's relatives include melons and squash.
Things that are usually green.Shrek: The green ogre of DreamWorks's 2001 film won the first-ever Oscar for Best Animated Feature.
Things that are usually green.Kermit the Frog: Kermit was first made by Jim Henson from his mother's old coat and ping-pong ball eyes, and he sings 'It's Not Easy Being Green'.
Things that are usually green.Pickle: A pickle is a cucumber cured in brine or vinegar, and it stays green thanks to the chlorophyll that survives the process.
Things that are usually green.Peas: Gregor Mendel's pea plants helped lay the foundations of genetics in the 1860s.
Things that are usually green.Lettuce: Lettuce is a relative of the sunflower and belongs to the daisy family.
Things that are usually green.Shamrock: Saint Patrick is said to have used the three-leaf clover to explain the Trinity, and it is Ireland's national emblem.
Things that are usually green.Spinach: Popeye's spinach habit was popularly blamed on a misplaced decimal point inflating its iron, though the story itself is partly myth.
Things that are usually green.The Hulk: Marvel's Hulk was originally gray in 1962, and printing problems pushed him to green.
Things that are usually green.Lemon: Lemons are yellow, but unripe ones are green, which makes them an almost-trap.
Things that are usually green.Ruby: Rubies are red because of chromium, and the same mineral in blue is sapphire, so neither is green.
Things that are usually green.Sapphire: Sapphire is the blue form of corundum, so it's blue, even though some rare ones turn out green or yellow.
Things that are usually green.Carrot: Carrots are orange, which is the opposite of green; the first domesticated carrots were purple or yellow.
Things that are usually green.Eggplant: Eggplant is usually purple, though some varieties are white or even green; the skin color comes from anthocyanin.
Things that are usually green.Tomato: A tomato is green when unripe and red when ripe; some heirlooms, like 'Green Zebra', stay green even when ripe.
Things that are usually green.Banana: Bananas are green when picked and ripen to yellow, and they are shipped green to avoid bruising.
Things that are usually green.Sky: The sky isn't green: air scatters blue light most, though a rare 'green flash' can appear at sunset.
Things that are usually green.Snow: Snow looks white because its ice crystals scatter all visible light equally, and it never looks green except in tinted algae snow.
Things that are usually green.Blueberry: Blueberries are blue only because of a waxy bloom, and their flesh is greenish, but they are not green.
Things that are usually green.Pumpkin: Pumpkins start green and ripen to orange, but the finished color is the one that counts.

Things with legs.Table: Ancient Egyptians and Romans both made tables with carved animal-paw legs, and a three-legged table is naturally stable on uneven floors.
Things with legs.Chair: Chair legs take the most wear at the joints, and for most of history chairs were seats of rank, with ordinary folk using stools or benches.
Things with legs.Tripod: Three legs always make a stable base, since any three points define a plane, which is why a tripod never wobbles on uneven ground.
Things with legs.Easel: Many easels have three legs, and the word comes from the Dutch ezel, meaning donkey, since it carries a load like a pack animal.
Things with legs.Grand piano: A grand piano stands on three legs, and a big concert model can weigh over 500 kilograms, hence the burly legs.
Things with legs.Stool: The three-legged milking stool is a classic design, as it never wobbles on uneven barn floors.
Things with legs.Ironing board: Ironing boards have folding legs in an X shape, and the design is credited to Sarah Boone, who patented an improved one in 1892.
Things with legs.Bed frame: Bed legs lift the mattress off the floor, and old four-poster beds were designed to keep sleepers away from drafts and bugs.
Things with legs.Desk: The word desk comes from the Latin discus, and the original desk was a board on legs, used by monks for writing.
Things with legs.Pants: Pants have two legs, and the garment was once worn by horse riders in Central Asia, and later spread across the world.
Things with legs.Sawhorse: A sawhorse is a four-legged trestle used to support wood, named after the horse it resembles in shape, though it never gallops.
Things with legs.Snake: Snakes evolved from legged lizards, and some, like pythons and boas, still carry tiny leftover hip bones and spurs.
Things with legs.Goldfish: A goldfish has fins, not legs, and a pet one can recognize its feeder, and live for decades with good care.
Things with legs.Rug: A rug lies flat on the floor, and some of the oldest knotted carpets were found in a Siberian tomb, from around 2,500 years ago.
Things with legs.Mirror: A hanging mirror just hangs on a wall, though a standing cheval mirror gets its name from the French word for horse.
Things with legs.Book: A book rests on a shelf with no legs, though people say that a really good one has them, meaning it keeps selling.
Things with legs.Door: A door hangs from hinges and so has no legs, though its frame has jambs on either side.
Things with legs.Pillow: Ancient Egyptians slept on carved stone or wood headrests, and soft pillows later spread, so the pillow has never needed legs.
Things with legs.Hammock: A hammock has no legs and hangs between two supports, and the Maya and Taino hung them to sleep above bugs and snakes.
Things with legs.Beanbag: The beanbag chair was designed in Italy in 1968 as the Sacco, and its filling shapes itself around the sitter, so it needs no legs.
Things with legs.Window: A window has a frame and sashes, no legs, though the word comes from the Old Norse for wind eye.
Things with legs.Curtain: A curtain hangs from a rod, and the word comes from the Latin for a small court, as in a hung enclosure.
Things with legs.Earthworm: An earthworm has no legs, and moves using bristles called setae, and its burrowing has been called the plow of nature by Darwin.
Things with legs.Slug: A slug glides on a single muscular foot lubricated by slime, and it has two pairs of tentacles with eyes on the longer top pair.

Skyscrapers.Burj Khalifa: Burj Khalifa in Dubai rises 828 metres and has been the world's tallest building since 2010.
Skyscrapers.Shanghai Tower: Shanghai Tower twists as it rises, which cuts the wind forces on it by roughly a quarter compared with a straight tower.
Skyscrapers.Taipei 101: Taipei 101 stabilizes itself in typhoons and quakes with a huge steel pendulum ball, weighing about 660 tonnes, that visitors can see.
Skyscrapers.Petronas Towers: The Petronas Towers in Kuala Lumpur were the world's tallest buildings from 1998 to 2004, linked by a double-decker skybridge.
Skyscrapers.Willis Tower: Willis Tower in Chicago was the Sears Tower and the world's tallest building for about 25 years from 1973, and its glass ledge hangs over the city.
Skyscrapers.Empire State: The Empire State Building opened in 1931 after only about a year of construction, which was astonishingly fast.
Skyscrapers.Chrysler Building: The Chrysler Building held the height record for just a few months in 1930, and its spire was secretly assembled inside the tower, then hoisted into place.
Skyscrapers.The Shard: The Shard in London, opened in 2012 and designed by Renzo Piano, is the tallest building in the UK at about 310 metres.
Skyscrapers.Merdeka 118: Merdeka 118 in Kuala Lumpur, completed in 2023, stands about 679 metres tall and is the world's second-tallest building.
Skyscrapers.Lotte World Tower: Lotte World Tower in Seoul has 123 floors and reaches 555 metres, making it South Korea's tallest building.
Skyscrapers.One World Trade: One World Trade Center stands 1,776 feet tall, a nod to the year of American independence.
Skyscrapers.Taj Mahal: The Taj Mahal is a marble mausoleum built in the 1600s for Mumtaz Mahal, and at about 73 metres it is monumental but no skyscraper.
Skyscrapers.Colosseum: The Colosseum is about 48 metres high and once held tens of thousands of spectators, but it is ancient Roman, not a skyscraper.
Skyscrapers.Parthenon: The Parthenon, built in the fifth century BCE in Athens, was a temple to Athena, and it was low-rise.
Skyscrapers.White House: The White House has 132 rooms but only a few floors, so it is hardly a skyscraper.
Skyscrapers.Louvre: The Louvre began as a medieval fortress before becoming the world's most visited museum, and it's wide rather than tall.
Skyscrapers.Sydney Opera House: The Sydney Opera House roof shells are covered in over a million tiles, but the building is not tall.
Skyscrapers.Pantheon: The Pantheon in Rome has a concrete dome that is still the largest unreinforced concrete dome ever built, but it is only about 43 metres high.
Skyscrapers.Alhambra: The Alhambra is a hilltop palace in Granada with delicate tilework, and it spreads out instead of up.
Skyscrapers.Hagia Sophia: Hagia Sophia in Istanbul held the title of the largest cathedral for almost a thousand years, but it is not a skyscraper.
Skyscrapers.Kremlin: The Kremlin is Moscow's fortified complex, and kreml simply means fortress.
Skyscrapers.Buckingham Palace: Buckingham Palace has about 775 rooms, but only a handful of floors, so it is not a skyscraper.
Skyscrapers.Guggenheim: The Guggenheim in New York is a spiral gallery by Frank Lloyd Wright, only a few stories high.
Skyscrapers.Notre-Dame: Notre-Dame in Paris has a spire of about 96 metres, rebuilt after the 2019 fire, but it is a cathedral, not a skyscraper.

Words that can come before \"hat\".Top: London hatter John Hetherington was reportedly fined in 1797 for causing a public disturbance by wearing a tall silk one.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Hard: Golden Gate Bridge crews were required to wear them in the 1930s, helping spread the hard hat from mines to every building site.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Sun: Dermatologists suggest a brim of at least three inches, enough to shade the face, ears and neck.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Cowboy: John B. Stetson designed his Boss of the Plains in 1865, and its wide brim and tall crown became the symbol of the American West.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Party: Its cone shape echoes the old dunce cap, yet this pointed headwear now signals birthdays and celebration instead of shame.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Bowler: Designed in 1849 by London hatmakers Thomas and William Bowler for a gamekeeper, who needed a hat that would survive branches.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Panama: Made in Ecuador, not Panama; it got its name because workers on the Panama Canal wore it and sellers shipped it through there.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Straw: Flat straw boaters were popular for river outings, and Luton in England was long a center of straw-hat making.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Bucket: The US Army issued a version as a jungle hat in the Vietnam era, which helped turn a fishing hat into a fashion staple.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Ten-gallon: It holds under a gallon of water, so the name is not about volume; one theory ties it to the Spanish galon, a braid.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Chef's: The classic toque has 100 pleats, said to stand for the 100 ways a chef can cook an egg.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Waist: Waistcoat is the one that works: it pairs with coat, and in British English the word means a vest worn under a jacket.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Pea: Pea coat is a short wool jacket long favored by sailors; the hat version does not exist as a word.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Trench: The trench coat was developed for officers in World War I; a trench hat, however, is not a word.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Petti: Petticoat comes from petty coat, a small coat, and it fits the word coat, not hat.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Over: Overcoat works because it is worn over everything else; overhat is not an English word.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Tail: Tailcoat has long back flaps and gave rise to the idiom coattails; it doesn't come before hat.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Turn: Turncoat is someone who changes sides, an idea tied to turning a coat inside out; it belongs to coat, not hat.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Shoe: Shoehorn exists, but shoehat does not; the horn in the name comes from the material it was once made of.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Neck: Neck pairs with tie, lace and line, but no one has ever worn a neck hat, so it fails the test.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Belly: Belly dance and belly button are real words, but belly hat is not, so this one is a trap.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Arm: Arm goes before chair, band and pit, but not before hat, so armhat is not a word.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Lab: Lab coat fits the coat test: scientists wear white coats because spills and stains show up clearly.
Words that can come before \"hat\".Wrist: Wristwatch and wristband are real, but wrist hat is not, since a hat sits on the head.

Fictional dogs.Snoopy: Snoopy, the beagle of Peanuts, imagines himself a World War I flying ace battling the Red Baron from his doghouse.
Fictional dogs.Scooby-Doo: Scooby-Doo is a Great Dane who debuted in 1969; his full name is Scoobert, and he'll do almost anything for a Scooby Snack.
Fictional dogs.Lassie: Lassie, a collie, was played by a male dog, Pal, and his descendants, over several generations of film and TV.
Fictional dogs.Odie: Odie, Garfield's dim-witted yellow beagle, is routinely kicked off the table by the cat.
Fictional dogs.Pluto: Pluto is Mickey's pet dog, and he is notable because, unlike Goofy, he doesn't speak.
Fictional dogs.Goofy: Goofy is a dog too, but he walks upright and talks, which makes his relation to pet Pluto a long-running question.
Fictional dogs.Clifford: Clifford the Big Red Dog began as a 1963 children's book; his author said his giant size came from a name nearly being 'Tiny'.
Fictional dogs.Toto: Toto is Dorothy's terrier in The Wizard of Oz; the film dog was a Cairn terrier named Terry, who was paid more than many human actors.
Fictional dogs.Brian Griffin: Brian Griffin, Family Guy's martini-drinking dog, talks and writes novels, unlike the family's other pets.
Fictional dogs.Gromit: Gromit never speaks but expresses everything through his brow; he is the beagle companion of Wallace in Aardman's claymation.
Fictional dogs.Bolt: Bolt is a white shepherd who thinks he has superpowers because he stars in a TV show, in Disney's 2008 film.
Fictional dogs.Dug: Dug, the golden retriever in Pixar's Up, wears a collar that translates his thoughts, and gets distracted by squirrels.
Fictional dogs.Bluey: Bluey is an Australian cattle dog from the Brisbane-set show that became a worldwide hit for children.
Fictional dogs.Copper: Copper is a young hound in Disney's The Fox and the Hound, who becomes friends with Tod, a fox.
Fictional dogs.Garfield: Garfield is a lazy orange cat who loves lasagna; Jim Davis created him in 1978.
Fictional dogs.Tom: Tom is the cat chasing Jerry; despite the chases, he rarely wins.
Fictional dogs.Sylvester: Sylvester is a cat who chases Tweety, famous for saying 'Sufferin' succotash'.
Fictional dogs.Wile E. Coyote: Wile E. Coyote is a coyote, a wild canine, not a dog, and Acme products always fail him.
Fictional dogs.Hobbes: Hobbes is Calvin's tiger, who looks stuffed to adults but alive to Calvin.
Fictional dogs.Scratchy: Scratchy is the cat in the Simpsons' cartoon The Itchy & Scratchy Show, who loses to the mouse Itchy.
Fictional dogs.Puss in Boots: Puss in Boots is a cat, in a tale by Charles Perrault from 1697, who tricks his way to riches for his master.
Fictional dogs.Felix: Felix the Cat dates to the silent-film era of the 1920s and was one of the first cartoon stars.
Fictional dogs.Tod: Tod is a fox, so he is not a dog, though he befriends the hound Copper.
Fictional dogs.Swiper: Swiper is a fox who steals things in Dora the Explorer, and is stopped by 'Swiper, no swiping!'.

Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).Jeopardy!: Contestants give answers in the form of a question; the show has run since 1964, and Ken Jennings won 74 games in a row.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).The Chase: A British quiz in which a team faces a ruthless Chaser, such as Mark Labbett, known as The Beast.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).Mastermind: Started in 1972 in Britain, contestants sit in a black leather chair, famously saying I've started so I'll finish.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).University Challenge: Britain's student quiz, with Bamber Gascoigne hosting it from 1962 to 1987, famous for tough starter questions.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).Pointless: A British quiz in which players want the obscure answer that no one in a hundred gave.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).QI: Short for Quite Interesting, a British panel quiz that was hosted by Stephen Fry, and then by Sandi Toksvig.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).Eggheads: Teams of ordinary people challenge a panel of quiz champions in this British show, with the champions called Eggheads.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).Only Connect: Contestants must find the link between seemingly unrelated clues, with the Connecting Wall being a famously fiendish round.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).The Weakest Link: The host's famous line is You are the weakest link, goodbye; contestants vote each other off.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).Fifteen to One: A long-running British quiz of fifteen contestants, with Sandi Toksvig and William G. Stewart.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).Blockbusters: A teen quiz where students ask for a letter, as in Can I have a P please Bob?
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).Deal or No Deal: A game of chance in which contestants open briefcases, with no skill or knowledge needed.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).The Price Is Right: A game show in which contestants guess prices, with Bob Barker hosting for 35 years.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).Big Brother: A reality show where housemates are filmed living together and voted out.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).Survivor: A reality competition on a remote island, with tribal votes.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).Love Island: Love Island is a dating reality show that puts singles in a villa to couple up, and viewers vote; no quizzing involved.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).American Idol: A talent competition, which is reality television and not a quiz.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).MasterChef: A cooking competition, which tests skill rather than knowledge.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).The Voice: A singing contest with judges in spinning chairs, not a quiz.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).The Apprentice: A business reality show where candidates are fired, not a quiz.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).The Bachelor: A dating reality show about roses and proposals, not a quiz.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).Gladiators: A physical contest with contenders against athletes, not a quiz.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).Wipeout: A show of obstacle courses where contestants get knocked into the water, with no trivia.
Quiz shows (not game or reality shows).Fear Factor: Contestants perform stunts and eat gross things, with no questions.
